q: Which sequence converts ethyl 4-oxopentanoate into 5-hydroxy-5-methylhexan-2-one?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr (excess), ether  3. TBAF, THF
h: The ketone must survive while the ester gains two methyl groups. Which carbonyl is more reactive toward CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, and how can you hide it?
w: The target keeps the ketone and turns the ester carbon into C(CH3)2OH, which needs two equivalents of CH3MgBr at the ester. A ketone is more reactive than an ester toward a Grignard reagent, so the ketone must be protected first. Ethylene glycol with catalytic acid converts the ketone into a cyclic acetal (esters do not form acetals). Excess CH3MgBr then adds twice to the ester (ester → ketone → 3° alkoxide), and aqueous acid both protonates the alkoxide and hydrolyzes the acetal back to the ketone: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. CH3MgBr (excess) 3. H3O+.
x: Without protection the ketone reacts first and fastest, so the ketone carbon also gains a methyl group and the product is mainly 2,5-dimethylhexane-2,5-diol.
Protection is correct, but LiAlH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride, not methyl: the ester becomes CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the product is 5-hydroxypentan-2-one.
TBSCl silylates alcohols, not ketones, so the ketone is left unprotected; CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr attacks both carbonyls and TBAF has nothing to remove.

q: Which pairing of functional group, protecting group, and removal conditions is correct?
c: ketone: cyclic acetal (HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH); removed with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
alcohol: Boc carbamate (Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N); removed with TBAF
amine: TBS ether (TBSCl, imidazole); removed with H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
aldehyde: Cbz carbamate (CbzCl, Et<sub>3</sub>N); removed with CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H
h: Match each protecting group to the atom it bonds to: acetals bond to a carbonyl carbon, silyl groups to O, carbamates to N.
w: A cyclic acetal is the standard protecting group for a ketone or aldehyde: it forms from ethylene glycol with an acid catalyst, survives bases, hydrides and organometallics, and is removed with aqueous acid (H3O+). Silyl ethers (TBS) protect alcohols and come off with fluoride (TBAF); carbamates (Boc, Cbz) protect amines, with Boc removed by CF3CO2H and Cbz by H2, Pd/C.
x: Boc is an amine protecting group (a carbamate on nitrogen), and TBAF removes silyl ethers, not Boc.
A TBS group protects an alcohol oxygen, not an amine, and it is removed with fluoride (TBAF), not hydrogenolysis.
A carbamate needs an N–H to form, so it cannot protect an aldehyde; aldehydes are protected as acetals.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: Two carbonyls are present, but only one changes. Which hydride reagent is too weak to reduce an ester?
w: Only the aldehyde is reduced to CH2OH; the methyl ester is untouched. NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones quickly but reacts with esters only very slowly, so it is chemoselective here. LiAlH4 is strong enough to reduce both groups.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces esters as well as aldehydes, so both groups become CH<sub>2</sub>OH (1,4-benzenedimethanol).
Clemmensen conditions reduce the aldehyde C=O all the way to CH<sub>3</sub>, giving methyl 4-methylbenzoate, not an alcohol.
A Grignard reagent adds a methyl group (and also attacks the ester), so the product would contain CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>, not CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

q: Which sequence converts ethyl hexanoate into 1-phenylhexan-1-ol?
c: 1. DIBAL-H, toluene, −78 °C  2. H<sub>2</sub>O  3. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>MgBr, ether  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  3. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>MgBr, ether  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: The target is a secondary alcohol: one H and one phenyl on the old ester carbon. Which reagent stops an ester at the aldehyde stage?
w: The old ester carbon must end up as CH(OH)Ph, so it needs exactly one hydride and one phenyl. DIBAL-H at −78 °C reduces an ester to an aldehyde (the tetrahedral aluminum intermediate does not collapse until workup), and PhMgBr then adds once to the aldehyde: 1. DIBAL-H, −78 °C 2. H2O 3. C6H5MgBr 4. H3O+. Esters cannot be stopped at the ketone with a Grignard reagent, and an alcohol made first cannot be "added to".
x: The ketone formed after the first addition is more reactive than the ester, so PhMgBr adds twice (1,1-diphenylhexan-1-ol); a Grignard route from an ester never gives a secondary alcohol with an H on carbon.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> takes the ester all the way to hexan-1-ol; PhMgBr then only deprotonates the OH (giving benzene) and adds no carbon.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce the ester, so PhMgBr meets the unchanged ester and adds twice, giving the tertiary diphenyl alcohol.

q: Which sequence converts 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one into 3-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexan-1-one?
h: The new ethyl group appears on the β-carbon of the enone. Which organometallic adds 1,4 rather than 1,2?
w: The ethyl group must bond to C3, the β-carbon of the α,β-unsaturated ketone, so this is a conjugate (1,4) addition. Lithium diorganocuprates (Gilman reagents) add 1,4 to enones; protonation of the enolate on workup gives the saturated ketone with a new quaternary C3: 1. (CH3CH2)2CuLi 2. H3O+.
x: Grignard reagents add mainly 1,2 to the C=O of an enone, giving the tertiary allylic alcohol 1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
Hydrogenation removes the C=C first; a saturated ketone is not a Michael acceptor, so the cuprate has no electrophilic C3 to attack.
LDA forms the enolate at C6 (α′), so ethyl bromide alkylates C6 (6-ethyl-3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one), not C3.

q: Which starting materials give the bicyclic enone shown by a Robinson annulation (Michael addition, then intramolecular aldol condensation)?
c: 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one + but-3-en-2-one (methyl vinyl ketone), NaOEt, EtOH, heat
h: Find the new enone C=C (formed by the aldol) and the bond to the quaternary ring-fusion carbon (formed by the Michael). The carbon that carries the methyl was the nucleophile.
w: Work backward. The C=C–C=O of the new ring came from an intramolecular aldol condensation between a methyl ketone (CH3 → the ring CH=) and the original ring C=O. The quaternary ring-fusion carbon with its methyl was the enolate carbon in the Michael step, and it added to the CH2= end of methyl vinyl ketone. So the donor is 2-methylcyclohexanone, alkylated at its more substituted α-carbon (the thermodynamic enolate under NaOEt), and the acceptor is but-3-en-2-one: 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one + methyl vinyl ketone.
x: With cyclohexanone the ring-fusion carbon carries an H, and the methyl from pent-3-en-2-one ends up on the new ring next to the fusion carbon, not on the fusion carbon.
The 1,3-dione gives the Wieland–Miescher ketone, which has a second C=O in the left-hand ring; the target has only one carbonyl.
Acetone enolate adds to C3 of the enone, so no quaternary carbon bearing a methyl forms at the ring fusion; the connectivity does not match.

q: Which sequence converts ethyl acetoacetate into 5-phenylpentan-2-one?
h: In the acetoacetic ester synthesis the product is CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. What is R here, and must it be an S<sub>N</sub>2-reactive halide?
w: The acetoacetic ester synthesis makes methyl ketones CH3C(=O)CH2–R: ethoxide removes the doubly activated α-H (pKa ≈ 11), the enolate does SN2 on R–X, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester and decarboxylates the β-keto acid. Here CH3C(=O)CH2–R = CH3C(=O)CH2CH2CH2Ph, so R = CH2CH2Ph and the halide is 2-phenylethyl bromide: 1. NaOEt 2. PhCH2CH2Br 3. H3O+, heat.
x: Benzyl bromide puts only one CH<sub>2</sub> between the new bond and the ring, giving 4-phenylbutan-2-one (one carbon short).
Decarboxylating first gives acetone, which has lost the second activating group; ethoxide only partly deprotonates acetone, so aldol reactions and multiple alkylations compete.
Bromobenzene cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 (backside attack is blocked by the ring), so the enolate is not phenylated.

q: Which sequence converts diethyl malonate into cyclopentanecarboxylic acid?
c: 1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt (1 equiv), Br(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br  2. NaOEt (1 equiv)  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
h: Count ring atoms: the malonate α-carbon becomes one ring carbon, and the dibromide supplies the rest.
w: In a malonic ester ring synthesis the malonate carbon is alkylated twice by the same dihalide: first intermolecularly, then (after a second deprotonation) intramolecularly. The ring contains the malonate carbon plus every CH2 of the dihalide, so a five-membered ring needs four CH2 groups, Br(CH2)4Br. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation then leave one CO2H on the ring: 1. NaOEt, Br(CH2)4Br 2. NaOEt 3. H3O+, heat.
x: 1,3-Dibromopropane supplies three CH<sub>2</sub> groups, which with the malonate carbon gives a four-membered ring (cyclobutanecarboxylic acid).
1,5-Dibromopentane gives a six-membered ring (cyclohexanecarboxylic acid).
Without the second equivalent of base the ring never closes; hydrolysis and decarboxylation give the open-chain 6-bromohexanoic acid.

q: A student plans to make 3-nitroacetophenone from benzene as shown. Why does the plan fail, and what fixes it?
c: Step 2 fails: Friedel–Crafts acylation does not occur on the strongly deactivated nitrobenzene ring; acylate first, then nitrate
Step 2 gives the para isomer because NO<sub>2</sub> is an ortho/para director; nitrate after acylation instead
Step 1 fails: nitration requires an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst; use HNO<sub>3</sub> with FeBr<sub>3</sub>
Step 2 fails: AlCl<sub>3</sub> reduces the nitro group to an amine; use FeCl<sub>3</sub> instead
h: Friedel–Crafts reactions have a list of rings they will not touch. Is a nitro-substituted ring on it?
w: Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation fail on rings bearing a strongly deactivating group (NO2, C=O, SO3H, CF3, NR3+), because the acylium ion is too weak an electrophile for such an electron-poor ring. Both substituents of the target are meta directors, so the order can simply be reversed: acylation of benzene gives acetophenone, and the acetyl group directs nitration meta. Step 2 fails; acylate first, then nitrate.
x: NO<sub>2</sub> is a meta director, not ortho/para; the real problem is that the deactivated ring does not undergo Friedel–Crafts acylation at all.
Nitration uses H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to generate NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>; FeBr<sub>3</sub> is the catalyst for bromination, and step 1 works as written.
AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid, not a reducing agent; the nitro group is left intact and simply shuts down the Friedel–Crafts reaction.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown (Stork enamine reaction)?
h: The enamine β-carbon is the nucleophile, and methyl acrylate is a Michael acceptor. What does aqueous acid do to an iminium ion?
w: Pyrrolidine and cyclohexanone form an enamine, a neutral enolate equivalent whose α-carbon is nucleophilic. It adds 1,4 to methyl acrylate (attack at the CH2= β-carbon), giving an iminium ion/enamine that aqueous acid hydrolyzes back to the ketone. The net result is Michael addition of cyclohexanone to methyl acrylate: methyl 3-(2-oxocyclohexyl)propanoate.
x: This is the enamine before hydrolysis; step 3 (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) converts the C=C–N unit back into the C=O.
Enamines add to the C=C of an α,β-unsaturated ester (conjugate addition); they do not substitute at the ester carbonyl to make an acryloyl ketone.
D has the new bond to the α-carbon of the acrylate; in a Michael addition the nucleophile attacks the β-carbon (the CH<sub>2</sub>= end).

q: Which sequence gives 1-bromo-3-propylbenzene from benzene?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
h: Br and propyl are meta to each other, yet both are ortho/para directors. Which group could you install that directs meta and later becomes propyl?
w: Both final groups are ortho/para directors, so neither can place the other meta. The trick is to introduce the propyl group as a propanoyl group: acylation (no rearrangement, and C=O is a meta director), then bromination meta to the ketone, then Clemmensen reduction of C=O to CH2: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3 3. Zn(Hg), HCl. Friedel–Crafts acylation also avoids the 1° carbocation rearrangement that ruins direct propylation.
x: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 1-chloropropane rearranges to the isopropyl cation (giving cumene), and the alkyl group then directs bromine ortho/para.
Reducing the ketone before bromination turns the meta director into propyl, an ortho/para director, so Br goes ortho/para.
Bromine is an ortho/para director, so the acylation occurs para to Br; the product is 1-bromo-4-propylbenzene.

q: Which sequence converts benzene into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. CuBr
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
h: Three bromines meta to one another cannot come from bromine directing itself. Which group directs to the three positions ortho/para to it, and can then be removed?
w: Bromine is an ortho/para director, so bromines cannot direct each other into a 1,3,5-pattern. An NH2 group is a powerful ortho/para director: aniline with Br2/H2O brominates both ortho positions and the para position, which are mutually meta (2,4,6-tribromoaniline). The NH2 is then removed by diazotization and reduction with hypophosphorous acid, which replaces N2+ by H: nitrate, reduce, brominate, NaNO2/HCl, H3PO2.
x: Each Br directs ortho/para, so the second and third bromines go ortho/para to the first (mainly 1,2,4-tribromobenzene), never all mutually meta.
CuBr (Sandmeyer) replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by Br instead of H, giving 1,2,3,5-tetrabromobenzene.
Bromination of nitrobenzene places only one Br meta; after reduction and deamination the product is bromobenzene.

q: Which sequence converts chlorobenzene into 4-methoxyaniline?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
1. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  3. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, heat  3. NaBH<sub>4</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH
h: Methoxide can replace Cl on a ring only by S<sub>N</sub>Ar. What must be on the ring, and where, while that step runs?
w: Cl is an ortho/para director, so nitration of chlorobenzene gives 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (separated from the ortho isomer). The para nitro group activates the C–Cl carbon toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution (addition–elimination through a Meisenheimer complex), so methoxide replaces Cl. Only then is the nitro group reduced to NH2: 1. HNO3, H2SO4 2. NaOCH3, heat 3. H2, Pd/C.
x: Plain chlorobenzene has no electron-withdrawing group to stabilize the Meisenheimer complex, so S<sub>N</sub>Ar with methoxide does not occur in step 1.
Reducing first converts the activating NO<sub>2</sub> into an electron-donating NH<sub>2</sub>, so the ring is no longer activated for S<sub>N</sub>Ar and step 3 fails.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce an aromatic nitro group; the product would remain 4-nitroanisole.

q: Which sequence converts 4-piperidinylmethanol into 4-(methoxymethyl)piperidine?
c: 1. Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. CbzCl, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Boc<sub>2</sub>O, Et<sub>3</sub>N  2. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Which is the better nucleophile toward CH<sub>3</sub>I, the ring N–H or the O–H? Then check that each protecting group comes off under the conditions chosen.
w: The secondary amine is more nucleophilic than the alcohol, so it would be methylated (and even quaternized) by CH3I. Protect it as a Boc carbamate, which has no N–H and is not nucleophilic. NaH then deprotonates only the OH, and the alkoxide is methylated (Williamson). Boc is acid-labile and is removed with trifluoroacetic acid: 1. Boc2O 2. NaH, CH3I 3. CF3CO2H.
x: With the amine unprotected, nitrogen competes for CH<sub>3</sub>I and gives N-methyl and quaternary ammonium products.
Cbz protects the amine, but it is stable to CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H; Cbz is removed by hydrogenolysis (H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C), so the final step fails.
Boc is not cleaved by hydrogenolysis; it needs acid (CF<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H), so the product would still carry the Boc group.

q: Which reagent removes the Boc group shown while leaving the benzyl ether intact?
h: Boc is the protecting group that leaves as a tert-butyl cation. What kind of reagent triggers that?
w: A Boc carbamate is cleaved by strong acid: protonation lets a tert-butyl cation leave (it becomes isobutylene), and the carbamic acid loses CO2 to free the amine. Benzyl ethers are stable to these conditions, so CF3CO2H is selective.
x: Hydrogenolysis cleaves benzyl–O bonds (and Cbz groups), so it would remove the benzyl ether and leave the Boc group.
Fluoride removes silyl ethers such as TBS; it does not cleave carbamates.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces aldehydes and ketones; it does not touch carbamates or ethers.

q: Which sequence converts 3-bromopropan-1-ol into 4-methylpentane-1,4-diol?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. TBAF, THF
1. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, TsOH (cat.)  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O; then NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq)  4. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: A Grignard reagent and an O–H cannot exist in the same flask. How do you hide an alcohol, and what takes the group off?
w: The new C–C bond joins C3 of the bromoalcohol to the carbonyl carbon of acetone, which calls for the Grignard reagent of the bromide. A free OH (pKa ≈ 16) would protonate the Grignard reagent immediately, so the alcohol is first protected as a TBS ether. The protected Grignard reagent adds to acetone, mild workup protonates the alkoxide, and fluoride removes the silyl group: 1. TBSCl 2. Mg 3. acetone; NH4Cl 4. TBAF.
x: The unprotected OH destroys the Grignard reagent by proton transfer, giving propan-1-ol (after workup) instead of adding to acetone.
Ethylene glycol/acid protects aldehydes and ketones as acetals; it does not protect an alcohol, so the OH still quenches the Grignard reagent.
H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C does not cleave silyl ethers, so the product keeps the TBS group on the primary oxygen.

q: Which reagent converts cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane?
c: Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> (from CH<sub>3</sub>PPh<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> Br<sup>−</sup> and n-BuLi), THF
h: You need a C=C exactly where the C=O was. Which reaction puts it there with no choice of position?
w: The Wittig reaction replaces C=O with C=C at the same carbon, so the double bond cannot migrate. Methylidenetriphenylphosphorane converts cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane via the oxaphosphetane, with Ph3P=O as by-product.
x: Acid dehydration of 1-methylcyclohexanol forms the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene, not the exocyclic alkene.
The enolate is methylated at the α-carbon, giving 2-methylcyclohexanone; the C=O is unchanged.
This stops at 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol; no alkene is formed.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 4-phenylbutan-2-ol?
h: Grignard reagents open epoxides at the less substituted carbon, and the OH ends up on the other epoxide carbon. Map each choice onto the target.
w: A Grignard reagent opens an epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered carbon, so the OH stays on the more substituted carbon and the chain grows by two carbons. Benzyl Grignard attacks the CH2 of 2-methyloxirane: PhCH2–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3, which is 4-phenylbutan-2-ol.
x: Phenyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of the epoxide, giving PhCH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> (1-phenylpropan-2-ol), one CH<sub>2</sub> short.
Methyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-benzyloxirane, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>Ph (1-phenylbutan-2-ol); the OH is next to the benzyl carbon.
Addition to acetone gives a tertiary alcohol, 2-methyl-4-phenylbutan-2-ol, with an extra methyl group.

q: Which sequence converts diethyl hexanedioate into 2-methylcyclopentan-1-one?
c: 1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. NaOEt, CH<sub>3</sub>I  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr (1 equiv); then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CuLi; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: A Dieckmann condensation of a 1,6-diester gives a five-membered β-keto ester. Where is the most acidic C–H, and what should happen to it before decarboxylation?
w: NaOEt cyclizes diethyl hexanedioate (Dieckmann) to ethyl 2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate. Its C–H between the two carbonyls (pKa ≈ 11) is easily deprotonated by ethoxide, and the enolate is methylated by CH3I. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester and decarboxylates the β-keto acid, leaving the methyl on the α-carbon: 1. NaOEt; H3O+ 2. NaOEt, CH3I 3. H3O+, heat.
x: After decarboxylation, CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr adds to the C=O of cyclopentanone, giving the tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.
CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr is a strong base: it removes the acidic α-H of the β-keto ester (making methane) instead of forming a C–C bond, so decarboxylation gives plain cyclopentanone.
Cyclopentanone is neither an enone nor an acid chloride, so the Gilman reagent does not react with it.

q: Which compound gives 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one on heating with NaOH (intramolecular aldol condensation)?
h: Number the carbons of the target ring. The enolate carbon and the carbonyl carbon it attacks must end up five atoms apart in the ring, and one carbonyl must remain.
w: In an intramolecular aldol the enolate carbon bonds to the other carbonyl carbon, which loses OH as water to form the C=C. For hexane-2,5-dione the terminal CH3 (C1) enolate attacks C5: the ring is C1–C2–C3–C4–C5 (five atoms), the C2 carbonyl stays, and dehydration puts the C=C conjugated with it, with C6 as the methyl on the alkene carbon. Hexane-2,5-dione gives 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one.
x: Heptane-2,6-dione closes a six-membered ring, giving 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.
The CH<sub>3</sub> enolate of 4-oxopentanal attacks the aldehyde to close a five-membered ring, but there is no extra carbon left for the methyl: the product is cyclopent-2-en-1-one.
Octane-2,7-dione closes a five-membered ring through its internal C3 enolate, giving 1-(2-methylcyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one, which keeps an acetyl group.
